subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.3, an extract on mid-latitude cyclones.

Name the type of climate that is found at the south-western tip of the country.
subQuestions.memoText: Mediterranean (climate)

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.3, an extract on mid-latitude cyclones.

Describe the climate experienced at the south-western tip of the country during winter as indicated in the extract.
subQuestions.memoText: Cool and wet (winters).

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.3, an extract on mid-latitude cyclones.

Why do mid-latitude cyclones migrate (move) further north in winter?
subQuestions.memoText: The shifting of the ITCZ causes mid-latitude cyclones to migrate further north in winter. The sun is now overhead of the Tropic of Cancer (northern hemisphere), and the apparent movement of the sun draws the pressure belts and the mid-latitude cyclones northward with it.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.3, an extract on mid-latitude cyclones.

Describe TWO changes in the weather associated with the passing of a cold front over Cape Town.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (2 marks each):
• Temperature decreases as the cold front passes.
• Atmospheric pressure decreases ahead of the cold front but increases in the cold sector behind it.
• Cloud cover increases and cumulonimbus clouds form, bringing heavy rain, snow, hail or thunderstorms.
• Humidity decreases behind the cold front.
• Wind direction changes (backs from north-west to south-west).
• Wind speed increases, bringing sudden gusty winds.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.3, an extract on mid-latitude cyclones.

In a paragraph of approximately EIGHT lines, explain the negative impact of cold fronts on tourism in Cape Town.
subQuestions.memoText: Cold fronts associated with mid-latitude cyclones bring heavy rainfall that can make tourist destinations in Cape Town inaccessible. Rock falls and landslides triggered by the heavy rain further reduce accessibility to popular tourist sites. Strong winds associated with cold fronts also make coastal and outdoor destinations dangerous, decreasing their accessibility. Rough seas and high waves decrease accessibility to coastal attractions and reduce business for tour operators who run boat trips and water-based excursions. Snow on the mountains makes hiking trails inaccessible, limiting outdoor tourism activities. Travel arrangements such as flights and sea travel are disrupted by the poor weather, inconveniencing tourists. The aesthetical appeal of tourist attractions is diminished by the bad weather, for example debris on beaches makes them unattractive. Cancellation of bookings due to poor weather results in reduced income for the tourism sector in Cape Town. [Any FOUR valid points × 2 marks each]

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.4 showing slope aspect.

Define the concept slope aspect.
subQuestions.memoText: Slope aspect is the direction in which a slope faces in relation to the sun's rays. / The angle at which the sun's rays strike the slope.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.4 showing slope aspect.

Does A or B represent the Southern Hemisphere?
subQuestions.memoText: B

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.4 showing slope aspect.

Give a reason evident from the sketch for your answer to QUESTION 1.4.2.
subQuestions.memoText: In the Southern Hemisphere (B) the north-facing slopes receive direct rays of the sun, as shown in the sketch. In the Northern Hemisphere (A) it is the south-facing slopes that receive the direct rays of the sun. / In the Southern Hemisphere (B) the south-facing slopes receive oblique rays of the sun.

subQuestions.label: 1.4.4 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.4 showing slope aspect.

How does slope aspect influence the microclimate of valley slopes with regard to temperature?
subQuestions.memoText: There is a difference in temperature between the slopes in a valley. The slope that faces the sun (north-facing in the Southern Hemisphere) will have a higher temperature due to receiving direct rays of the sun. The slope that faces away from the sun (south-facing in the Southern Hemisphere) will have a lower temperature as it receives oblique rays.

subQuestions.label: 1.4.4 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.4 showing slope aspect.

How does slope aspect influence the microclimate of valley slopes with regard to evaporation?
subQuestions.memoText: Evaporation rates differ on each slope. The slope that faces the sun will have a higher evaporation rate and will be drier. The slope that faces away from the sun will have a lower evaporation rate and will have a higher moisture content.

subQuestions.label: 1.4.5 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.4 showing slope aspect.

Explain the influence of slope aspect in the Southern Hemisphere on farming.
subQuestions.memoText: Different types of crops have to be grown on the north- and south-facing slopes because of the difference in temperature and moisture. North-facing slopes in the Southern Hemisphere favour the growth of crops that require more sunlight and less moisture, such as citrus fruit and thick-skinned fruit. South-facing slopes encourage the growth of products that require cooler conditions with more moisture.

subQuestions.label: 1.4.5 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.4 showing slope aspect.

Explain the influence of slope aspect in the Southern Hemisphere on human settlements.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (must refer to specific slope, 2 marks each):
• People prefer to settle on the warmer north-facing slopes in the Southern Hemisphere as these receive direct rays of the sun and are warmer.
• Residents on north-facing slopes save on energy costs as less heating is required.
• South-facing slopes are colder and not ideal for human settlement as they receive only oblique rays of the sun.
• South-facing slopes require more and expensive heating methods, increasing the cost of settlements.
• South-facing slopes receive more precipitation and fog and are therefore not favourable for human settlement.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.5 showing drainage density.

Define the concept drainage density.
subQuestions.memoText: Drainage density is the relationship between the total length of streams and the area drained in a drainage basin. / The total length of streams per unit area.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.5 showing drainage density.

State the difference in drainage density of drainage basins A and B.
subQuestions.memoText: Drainage basin A has a lower drainage density (fewer stream channels per unit area), while drainage basin B has a higher drainage density (more stream channels per unit area).

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.5 showing drainage density.

How did rock permeability influence the drainage density of drainage basin A?
subQuestions.memoText: The rocks in drainage basin A are more permeable, which allows for more infiltration and less surface runoff. Because more water infiltrates into the ground rather than flowing over the surface, fewer stream channels are formed, resulting in a lower drainage density.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.5 showing drainage density.

Determine the stream order of the river system in drainage basin A at point X.
subQuestions.memoText: 2nd (second) order stream.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.5 showing drainage density.

Describe the relationship between drainage density and stream order of a river by referring to drainage basins A and B.
subQuestions.memoText: At drainage basin A, the drainage density is low and the stream order is correspondingly low. At drainage basin B, the drainage density is high and the stream order is also high. This shows a positive relationship — as drainage density increases, so does the stream order. Areas with more stream channels (higher drainage density) develop higher-order river systems.

subQuestions.label: 1.5.6 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.5 showing drainage density.

Explain how a steep gradient influences the drainage density in drainage basin B.
subQuestions.memoText: Steeper gradients increase the velocity (speed) of the water, resulting in higher runoff and discharge. This increased runoff creates more stream channels and therefore a higher drainage density in drainage basin B.

subQuestions.label: 1.5.6 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.5 showing drainage density.

Explain how an increase in precipitation influences the drainage density in drainage basin B.
subQuestions.memoText: Increasing precipitation increases the volume of water and runoff/discharge in the basin. This greater volume of water creates more stream channels, resulting in a higher drainage density in drainage basin B.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.6 showing river capture (stream piracy).

Is river X or Y the captured river?
subQuestions.memoText: River Y is the captured river.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.6 showing river capture (stream piracy).

Give TWO pieces of evidence in diagram B that show that river capture has taken place.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (1 mark each):
• A wind gap is visible where the original valley of river Y continues dry.
• An elbow of capture (sharp bend) is visible where river Y was diverted.
• A misfit stream is present in the lower valley of river Y, which is too small for the valley it occupies.
• River gravel from the upper course of river Y is found beyond the watershed.
• The captor/pirate stream (river X or W) has a greater volume of water.
• The watershed between river X and Y has been eroded.
• The water in the upper stream of river Y is diverted to river X.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.6 showing river capture (stream piracy).

What influence does the underlying rock have on river capture?
subQuestions.memoText: Rivers that flow over softer or less resistant rock cause an increase in headward erosion, making it easier for the captor stream to cut through the watershed and capture the adjacent river. Rivers that flow over hard or more resistant rock limits headward erosion and slows down the process of river capture.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.6 showing river capture (stream piracy).

How does river capture rejuvenate the captor stream?
subQuestions.memoText: River capture increases the volume of water in the captor stream, which increases the river's erosive power. The increasing velocity of the water results in more erosive ability and re-energises the captor stream, allowing it to erode more deeply and transport more sediment.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 1.6 showing river capture (stream piracy).

In a paragraph of approximately EIGHT lines, discuss how river capture will have a positive impact on farming at W.
subQuestions.memoText: River capture will have several positive impacts on farming at W. More water will be available at W through weirs, canals, furrows and water points, making water accessible for irrigation farming. Silt will be deposited on the floodplain around W, resulting in more fertile soil and increasing the area available for large-scale crop farming. The increased farming activity at W will create more employment opportunities for farm workers. Greater agricultural production at W will result in higher profits and increased exports, benefiting the local economy. Infrastructure such as roads and storage facilities will be improved to support the increased farming activities. Industries linked to agriculture, such as food processing plants and storage facilities, will be encouraged to establish in the area. Increased production will lead to greater food security in the region. More water will also be available to generate hydro-electricity to supply power to farms and to create more grazing land for livestock farming. [Any FOUR valid points × 2 marks each]

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 2.3 showing a synoptic weather map of Southern Africa.

Give evidence that the synoptic weather map represents a summer condition.
subQuestions.memoText: Any ONE of the following: A thermal/heat low is present over the interior; the South Indian High and South Atlantic High are in a southerly position; high temperatures exist over the interior; overcast/cloudy conditions are present over the interior; a dominant low pressure is evident in the interior.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 2.3 showing a synoptic weather map of Southern Africa.

Determine the isobaric interval on the synoptic weather map.
subQuestions.memoText: 4 hPa/mb

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 2.3 showing a synoptic weather map of Southern Africa.

Name the high-pressure cell A.
subQuestions.memoText: South Indian (High) / Mauritius Anticyclone

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 2.3 showing a synoptic weather map of Southern Africa.

State the wind direction and wind speed of the weather station at Durban.
subQuestions.memoText:
Wind direction: South-east (south-easterly).
Wind speed: 5 knots.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 2.3 showing a synoptic weather map of Southern Africa.

Comment on the relationship between wind speed and the arrangement of the isobars in the eastern half of the country.
subQuestions.memoText: The isobars in the eastern half of the country are far apart, indicating a gentle pressure gradient. A gentle pressure gradient results in low wind speeds. Therefore, the wind speed in the eastern half of the country is low because the isobars are widely spaced.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to FIGURE 2.3 showing a synoptic weather map of Southern Africa.

In a paragraph of approximately EIGHT lines, explain how high-pressure cell A and the low-pressure cell in the interior of the country could contribute to increased rainfall in the eastern half of the country during summer.
subQuestions.memoText: The South Indian High-pressure cell A is located further south and away from the land in summer. The on-shore winds from the South Indian High have a larger fetch as they are located further south in summer, allowing them to pick up more moisture over the warm Indian Ocean. More water is evaporated over the warm Indian Ocean, resulting in moisture-laden air. The moisture-laden air from the South Indian High rises and advects towards the thermal/heat low-pressure cell in the interior of the country. Intense heating over the land in summer causes thermal/heat low pressures to develop in the interior. The moist air is drawn towards the interior low, where it rises and cools. As the air rises, it becomes unstable, and convectional rainfall and thunderstorms develop, contributing to increased rainfall in the eastern half of the country during summer. [Any FOUR valid points × 2 marks each]

subQuestions.questionText:
Read the blog (journal entry) in FIGURE 2.4 based on South African berg winds.

According to the blog, on which side of the mountain do berg winds descend?
subQuestions.memoText: Leeward (side)

subQuestions.questionText:
Read the blog (journal entry) in FIGURE 2.4 based on South African berg winds.

Name the high-pressure system referred to in the blog.
subQuestions.memoText: Kalahari (High) / Continental (High)

subQuestions.label: 2.4.3 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Read the blog (journal entry) in FIGURE 2.4 based on South African berg winds. Berg winds are associated with the presence of a coastal low pressure.

What is a coastal low pressure?
subQuestions.memoText: A coastal low pressure is a small/weak low-pressure cell that is found along the coast.

subQuestions.label: 2.4.3 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
Read the blog (journal entry) in FIGURE 2.4 based on South African berg winds. Berg winds are associated with the presence of a coastal low pressure.

What role does a coastal low pressure play in the formation of berg winds?
subQuestions.memoText: The movement of air is channelled from the interior towards the coast. A pressure gradient develops between the Kalahari High in the interior and the coastal low, which drives the berg wind from the high-pressure interior down towards the low-pressure coast.

subQuestions.label: 2.4.3 (c)
subQuestions.questionText:
Read the blog (journal entry) in FIGURE 2.4 based on South African berg winds. Berg winds are associated with the presence of a coastal low pressure.

Why are berg winds associated with high temperatures?
subQuestions.memoText: Berg winds descend from the high interior plateau towards the coast. As the air descends, it is compressed and undergoes adiabatic heating, warming at the dry adiabatic lapse rate of approximately 1°C per 100 m of descent. This adiabatic heating results in very high temperatures at the coast.

subQuestions.questionText:
Read the blog (journal entry) in FIGURE 2.4 based on South African berg winds.

Explain the negative economic impact of the fires mentioned in the blog on farming in the area.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (2 marks each):
• Damaged crops decrease the production available to sell on local and international markets, reducing income.
• A decrease in crops results in lower profits, causing financial instability for farmers.
• Livestock are killed in the fires, resulting in lower production and financial losses.
• Grazing land is destroyed, causing livestock to die or be sold at reduced prices.
• Fires destroy farm buildings and machinery, resulting in costly repairs and insurance claims.
• The risk of fire leads to farmers paying higher insurance premiums, increasing production costs.
• Farmers may be forced to abandon their farms and seek employment elsewhere.
• Increase in unemployment due to decline in production on farms.

subQuestions.questionText:
Read the blog (journal entry) in FIGURE 2.4 based on South African berg winds.

Suggest strategies that farmers could implement to reduce the effects of fires associated with berg winds.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (2 marks each):
• Conduct awareness and education programmes amongst farm workers on fire prevention.
• Erect watch towers to provide early detection of fires.
• Farmers should equip themselves with fire-fighting equipment such as water tankers and pumps.
• Create fire breaks around the farm to prevent fires from spreading.
• Build sheds to keep livestock safe from fires.
• Build storage dams or reservoirs to ensure water is available to fight fires.
• Form partnerships with neighbouring farmers for coordinated fire-fighting responses.
• Install fire warning systems or alarms for early detection.
• Install sprinkler systems to protect crops and structures.

subQuestions.questionText:
FIGURE 2.5 illustrates drainage patterns.

Define the concept drainage pattern.
subQuestions.memoText: A drainage pattern is the arrangement of streams in a drainage basin.

subQuestions.questionText:
FIGURE 2.5 illustrates drainage patterns.

Identify drainage patterns A and B.
subQuestions.memoText:
Drainage pattern A – Dendritic (tree-like).
Drainage pattern B – Radial (centrifugal).

subQuestions.questionText:
FIGURE 2.5 illustrates drainage patterns.

Give TWO characteristics of drainage pattern A evident in FIGURE 2.5.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (1 mark each):
• Resembles the branches of a tree.
• Tributaries join the main stream at acute angles.
• Forms on rocks that are uniformly resistant to erosion.
• Forms on horizontally layered sedimentary rock.

subQuestions.questionText:
FIGURE 2.5 illustrates drainage patterns.

How does the volcanic landscape in FIGURE 2.5 result in drainage pattern B?
subQuestions.memoText: The volcanic landscape creates a dome-shaped feature. Rivers originate at the top of the dome (source) and radiate outwards and downslope in all directions from the central high point, forming the radial (centrifugal) drainage pattern.

subQuestions.questionText:
FIGURE 2.5 illustrates drainage patterns.

Why is drainage pattern A more suitable for settlements?
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (2 marks each):
• The land underlain by horizontally layered sedimentary rock is generally flat, making it suitable and safe for the construction of settlements.
• The tributaries of the dendritic drainage pattern are arranged so that water is accessible throughout the drainage basin, making it easy to obtain water for domestic use and irrigation.
• The flat terrain reduces the cost of construction and provides stable foundations for buildings.
• The gentle gradients associated with dendritic drainage reduce the risk of flooding for settlements.

subQuestions.questionText:
FIGURE 2.5 illustrates drainage patterns.

Explain how the characteristics of the underlying rock structure result in the formation of drainage patterns A and B.
subQuestions.memoText:
Drainage Pattern A (dendritic): Massive igneous and horizontally layered sedimentary rocks that are uniformly resistant to erosion cause tributaries to join the main stream at acute angles, forming the branching tree-like pattern. The uniform resistance to erosion results in tributaries of similar length, giving the pattern its symmetrical appearance.

Drainage Pattern B (radial): Massive igneous rocks in a dome shape cause rivers to flow outward from the central high point. The dome feature causes rivers to radiate downwards in all directions from the summit, forming the radial drainage pattern.

subQuestions.questionText:
FIGURE 2.6 illustrates fluvial landforms.

Which stage (course) of the river is illustrated in FIGURE 2.6?
subQuestions.memoText: Lower (course) / Old stage / Plain stage.

subQuestions.questionText:
FIGURE 2.6 illustrates fluvial landforms.

What role did the gradual gradient play in the formation of the meander evident in the sketch?
subQuestions.memoText: The gradual/gentle gradient decreases the velocity of the water. The reduced velocity causes the river to lose its ability to erode vertically and instead begins to erode laterally, cutting through less resistant rock on the sides, which causes the river to develop meanders.

subQuestions.questionText:
FIGURE 2.6 illustrates fluvial landforms.

Explain the formation of the undercut slope (outer bank) and slip-off slope (inner bank).
subQuestions.memoText:
Undercut slope (outer bank): Water flows faster on the outer bank of the meander due to centrifugal force. The faster-flowing water has greater erosive power and removes material through hydraulic action and abrasion, undercutting the outer bank and forming a steep undercut (concave) slope.

Slip-off slope (inner bank): On the inner bank, the water velocity is slower. The reduced velocity causes the river to deposit its sediment load on the inner bank, gradually building up a gentle slip-off (convex) slope.

subQuestions.questionText:
FIGURE 2.6 illustrates fluvial landforms.

In a paragraph of approximately EIGHT lines, explain how a meander develops into an oxbow lake.
subQuestions.memoText: Faster-flowing water on the outer banks of adjacent meander bends causes erosion and undercutting, while slower-moving water deposits material on the inner banks, forming slip-off slopes. The meander neck — the narrow strip of land between two adjacent bends — continuously narrows due to ongoing lateral erosion on the outer banks and deposition on the inner banks. During periods of heavy rainfall or flooding, when there is a significant increase in the volume and velocity of water, the river breaks through the narrow meander neck, taking the shorter, more direct route. The meander loop is now cut off and separated from the main river channel. The main river develops a straighter course through the breach. Deposition of sediment gradually seals off both ends of the cut-off meander loop. The isolated body of water remaining in the cut-off loop is now known as an oxbow lake. Over time, the oxbow lake may dry up and become a meander scar. [Any FOUR valid points × 2 marks each]
